proposed_edges.relationship: Lawrence Stone supervised Laqueur’s Princeton doctorate, awarded in 1973, as recorded in the contributor note to The First Modern Society (1989).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh OCR reading of the Cambridge publisher’s front matter, printed p. xviii (PDF p. 16), Laqueur contributor paragraph: “supervised by Lawrence Stone at Princeton”. The copyright leaf (PDF p. 5) distinguishes first publication in 1989 from this 2005 paperback. The freshly checked Berkeley Education section supplies the 1973 Ph.D. award date. A documented training relationship, classified as influence; no specific theoretical transmission is inferred. The festschrift chapters and dissertation remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Desan and Ragan’s 2002 AHA biography credits Laqueur and Lynn Hunt, alongside Stephen Greenblatt and other Berkeley colleagues, with collaborating to found Representations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Suzanne Desan and Bryant T. Ragan’s AHA presidential biography, Biography section, paragraph beginning “Yet it was in many ways a traditional monograph” and continuing through the paragraph beginning “As she explored”. The latter explicitly includes Laqueur among the colleagues with whom Hunt collaborated “to found the journal Representations”. Institutional biographical attribution of a shared editorial undertaking, not co-authorship of Hunt’s books or proof of reciprocal theoretical influence. Other founders retain credit. The founding documents themselves remain unread; the journal’s current Editors’ Statement supplies context only.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Me, Myself, and I” (2004), Greenblatt uses Laqueur’s Solitary Sex (2003) to interpret literary representations of masturbation from Shakespeare’s sonnets to Proust.
proposed_edges.map_label: Solitary Sex used in literary interpretation
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary Greenblatt review freshly read in publisher HTML: section 2, paragraphs beginning “In one of his early sonnets” through “Still, a poem like Shakespeare’s”; section 3, final paragraphs beginning “I confess” through “Still, Laqueur’s courageous cultural history”. Greenblatt connects Shakespeare’s procreative thrift to Laqueur’s distinction and explicitly paraphrases Laqueur when interpreting Proust. The phrase “chronicles so richly” marks positive reception. This is a specific critical use, not a claim that Laqueur originated Greenblatt’s method. Solitary Sex itself remains unread in full; its original 2003 date is independently confirmed by Berkeley’s bibliography.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: it is as if we had reentered the cultural world that Laqueur chronicles so richly
review.reason: NYRB April 8, 2004 issue, review of Solitary Sex. Section 2 links Shakespeare's sonnet to 'a recurrent theme in the history of “modern masturbation” that concerns Laqueur'; section 3 Proust passage and 'to paraphrase Laqueur's book'; 'Laqueur's courageous cultural history'. Better-supported addition: the opening calls Laqueur 'my friend and former Berkeley colleague', which could be noted. This is reception in a commissioned review, so the edge records a reviewer's interpretive use, as the sentence says.

proposed_edges.relationship: Chamboredon’s 1979 review presents Laqueur’s Religion and Respectability (1976) as a challenge to the Sunday-school indoctrination and working-class control thesis associated with Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Jean-Claude Chamboredon’s own review, printed p. 1268, opening paragraph and following discussion, freshly read in Persée’s page text. He explicitly names Thompson’s 1963 book and describes the thesis of Sunday schools as an instrument of indoctrination and control. Crucially, he also calls the thesis “forcée et schématisée” for Laqueur’s rebuttal: his reservation about Laqueur’s framing is retained, not treated as endorsement. The reviewed book’s original 1976 date is independently verified in Berkeley’s bibliography. Neither book nor the review’s pp. 1269–1275 was read; no quotation is attributed directly to either book.

review.reason: Annales 34:6 (1979), p. 1268 opening: thesis that Sunday schools were 'un instrument d'endoctrinement et de contrôle'; the book 'conduit à contredire cette thèse qui a été forcée et schématisée pour les besoins du démenti'.
